analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal approval of natural gas export applications and requires public reporting of where exported LNG goes.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it was referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee on June 18, 2014 and died there when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the Energy Department to decide natural gas export applications within 45 days after the environmental review ends. Challenges would go to one appeals court near the export facility, on an expedited schedule, and the court could order a decision within 30 days if the agency dragged its feet. It would also require companies to report which countries receive exported liquefied natural gas, with DOE posting that list publicly. The export-approval machinery it would speed up is the industry's main bottleneck; the disclosure requirement is a small transparency win.
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas producers and companies seeking licenses to export liquefied natural gas gain the most: a hard 45-day decision deadline after the environmental review, a court that must order a decision within 30 days if the agency misses deadlines, and challenges funneled to a single court on a fast docket. Consumers get one genuine benefit — DOE would have to publish which countries receive exported LNG [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Natural gas producers and LNG exporters

how_it_helps.text: DOE would have to issue a final decision on any pending or new export application within 45 days after the National Environmental Policy Act review concludes, ending the multi-year waits applicants faced.

Review of DOE decisions — or DOE's failure to decide — would go to the appeals court where the export facility is located, on original and exclusive jurisdiction, moving challenges out of the D.C. Circuit where they are normally heard.
If a court finds DOE failed to decide, it must order a decision within 30 days, and every such case gets expedited docketing, so opponents could not slow applications through extended litigation.
The bill adds a transparency measure: LNG exporters must report the destination countries of their cargoes, and DOE must publish the information on its website.

analysis.who_pays: The bill does not itself approve any export; but by forcing faster decisions it would accelerate the pace of LNG export licensing. More exports mean more American gas sold abroad, which tends to bid up domestic prices paid by households for heating and by utilities and manufacturers for power and feedstock. The shortened timelines and single-court review also shrink the room for affected communities and opponents to contest approvals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and businesses buying natural gas

drawbacks.text: The 45-day decision clock leaves DOE little time to weigh whether exporting the gas serves the public interest, a judgment the Natural Gas Act requires it to make.
Concentrating all review in one court near the facility, with mandatory expedited dockets, limits where opponents of a project can be heard and speeds cases past thorough litigation.
Expanded natural gas exports tend to raise domestic gas prices, which flows through to home heating bills and electricity costs; the bill contains no offsetting protection for consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provision is real but small — knowing where cargoes go does not change prices or approvals. The bill's core effect is to remove the two main sources of delay in export licensing: the agency's own pace and litigation. Exporters gain certainty worth billions; the cost is distributed across every household and factory that buys gas, through higher prices that economists broadly associate with expanded exports. An honest supporter would have to concede the bill trades a diffuse consumer cost for a concentrated industry benefit, softened only by the disclosure rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up, and the Congress ended with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Udall introduced the bill on June 18, 2014, with Sens. Mary Landrieu and Mark Begich joining as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's history before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: LNG exporters kept facing DOE's slower, case-by-case approval process and the usual litigation avenues, while domestic gas consumers avoided a licensing fast-track that would likely have pushed home heating and electricity prices higher. The bill's one public-facing idea — disclosing export destinations — also went nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Domestic gas consumers; exporters gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to speed DOE decisions on natural gas export applications and require disclosure of LNG destinations.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no roll-call or recorded opposition exists because the bill never left committee, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and LNG export developers
industries.note: The bill would fast-track the export licenses these companies need, with a 45-day decision deadline, mandatory court orders if the agency delays, and challenges confined to one expedited court. Faster approvals mean more gas sold abroad, which tends to raise the domestic prices ordinary households and businesses pay.

These industries buy large volumes of domestic natural gas, so accelerated export licensing that pushes up domestic prices raises their costs just as it raises consumers' heating and electric bills. They had no recorded role in this bill's brief life.
